summary: Number programs, build a universal evaluator, and distinguish recognizing successful computations from deciding whether they ever succeed.
abstract: Running a program may eventually show that it halts, but can another program always predict whether it will finish? Numbering the programs of the recursive-function model gives a universal simulator that performs any indexed computation and also runs forever when that computation does. Fixed inputs can be inserted into program text by a terminating transformation, yet no terminating algorithm decides halting for every program and input. Successful runs still have finite records that a program can check. This characterizes the computably enumerable sets: their members can be recognized by a search that halts on positive instances and may continue forever on negative ones. A set admits a decision procedure exactly when separate searches can recognize both members and nonmembers, making the boundary between simulation, recognition and decision precise.
